item.title: Tax attorney: Investor interest growing in CNMI incentive programs

item.content:encoded:
Tina Azarvand, managing partner of Azarvand Tax Law, said mainland investors are expressing growing interest in relocating businesses to the Northern Mariana Islands through the Commonwealth Economic Incentive Act and the Commonwealth Economic Development Authority's Qualifying Certificate program, though many are waiting to see how the newer incentive program is implemented.

Azarvand said she has discussed CNMI investment opportunities with clients who initially sought information about Puerto Rico's tax incentives but became interested in exploring the commonwealth's programs.

"There is definitely interest in the CNMI," she said, noting that one prospective investor traveled from Florida to visit the islands and evaluate opportunities firsthand.

Among those expressing interest are two firms considering operations in the CNMI. One is involved in private equity with a broad range of investment interests, while the other focuses on service-based businesses that can operate remotely and export services outside the islands, she said.

Azarvand declined to identify the companies, saying discussions remain ongoing.

The firms initially viewed CEDA's QC program as their primary incentive option. The QC program provides qualifying businesses tax benefits in exchange for investments that support economic development in the CNMI.

They are now also evaluating opportunities under the economic incentive act, a recently enacted program aimed at attracting new investment and business relocation through additional tax-related benefits.

"They've kind of been wanting to see how this CEIA incentive program goes and see the viability for them as well," Azarvand said.

Azarvand said awareness of the CNMI's incentive programs remains limited among tax professionals on the mainland, including attorneys who specialize in Puerto Rico tax incentives.

"Most tax attorneys I speak with don't even know of the CNMI Qualifying Certificate program," she said.

She said that lack of awareness presents an opportunity for the CNMI to market its incentive programs more aggressively as officials seek to diversify the economy and attract new private-sector investment.

item.title: Federal judge rules against administration in American Samoa seabed mining lease

item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.title: NWS urges vigilance as dry season begins across Guam and CNMI
item.description: The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal. A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade
item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal.

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade winds, according to the National Weather Service in Guam. Fire danger on Guam has risen to the high category as rainfall remains limited and vegetation continues to dry out.

Despite the dry conditions, Marcus Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Guam office, said residents should not overlook the threat of tropical cyclones.

"The risk for late-season tropical cyclones remains elevated through the end of the year and into early 2027 compared with other years," Aydlett said, citing the ongoing El Niño pattern.

No tropical cyclone development is expected during the next seven days, but forecasters said El Niño conditions could continue to influence weather across the western Pacific through the remainder of the year.

The weather service said a wetter pattern may develop later next week and continue into December, providing some relief to drought-affected areas across Micronesia. Residents with low or empty water catchments are encouraged to collect rainwater when showers occur.

item.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
item.description: NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.

Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – The only known draft of one of the most famous speeches in American history is on public display for the first time: The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s remarks at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963. And it's written in his own hand.

"Just for a few days we have this incredible artifact here, which is Doctor King's handwritten, final draft of what became known as the 'I Have a Dream' speech," said Jill Savitt, CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, King's hometown.

"Nothing has given me chills like this handwritten document, where you see him crafting one of the most iconic speeches in U.S. history."

It's written in cursive, blue ink on yellow legal paper. King scratched through entire sections and reworked them, or changed a particular word or phrase.

"You see him on the page wrestling with the words," Savitt said. "He's struggling with: How do you make this case to America that we're not living up to our own ideals?"

The seven-page document, which will be on exhibit here through Sunday, is enclosed in a glass case in a gallery dedicated to the March on Washington. Above the display, footage plays of speeches and the crowd of 250,000 gathered on the National Mall on Aug. 28, 1963.

Savitt said King originally titled the speech "Normalcy Never Again." Notably, the manuscript does not include what became the most famous lines from that day, "I Have a Dream."

"Doctor King improvised that," she said. "The preacher in him connected with a crowd in a particular way. And when you watch footage, you can almost see this electric charge go through him."

His rousing words that day on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial included:

"I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream today."

Savitt says King sent the draft to be typed up in the pre-dawn hours from the Willard Hotel in Washington, DC, on the day he was to deliver it.

The handwritten copy of King's speech was discovered by Xernona Clayton, an Atlanta civil rights leader who worked closely with King and his wife, Coretta Scott King. Her late husband, Edward Clayton, was one of King's speechwriters.

Now 96, she said in an interview with NPR Thursday she found the papers tucked in a manilla envelope while cleaning out his old desk.

"I knew Doctor King's handwriting very well, and I said, 'Oh, this can't be the speech,'" she recalled. "Then when I started reading it, I knew that it was and then I got scared. Like, what do I do now?"

That was in the late 1990s, and she tucked it back into the desk. She rediscovered it a couple years ago, and it took her back to 1963.

"As I went through the speech, I was reading his words and hearing them in my head," she said. "Martin Luther King spoke to the world through that speech."

She decided it was time to share the document with the world. Clayton's charitable trust is offering it for auction through Christie's in New York in January, where the auction house says bids could top $10 million. Prior to that, the manuscript also will be on display in Chicago.

Clayton said she wanted it available to the public with the hope that people will find inspiration in King's words today.

"He used to tell me all the time how much he hated that we as a people can't live together," she recalled. "That was his preachment. All of the time he was preoccupied with what can we do to get people to love each other."

For former Atlanta Mayor Shirley Franklin, who visited the center last week, seeing the document was personal.

"Do you see me?" she asked, pointing to a photograph on display of the crowd at the March on Washington. "I'm sitting right there by the reflecting pool."

Franklin was Atlanta's mayor from 2002-2010, the first Black woman elected to lead a city in the Deep South.

"It's amazing that 60 years later this document has survived," she said.

Looking at King's writings, Franklin said she was struck by how thoughtful he was about each and every word.

"As brilliant as he was, as clear as he was about what he was trying to accomplish, it required enhancement and refinement," she said. "He was making this speech as good as it could be."

Yet even with all the reviewing and refining, what stuck from that speech never made it on the paper.

"What we remember is the part that came from his heart," Franklin said. "Gives me the chills."

Franklin is a living witness to the change wrought by the work of King and others civil rights pioneers, but she said seeing the speech is a reminder that the work is ongoing.

"Sixty years later, we've made some progress," she said. "Much of what he says is relevant today, because we've not really fulfilled the full promise of a free and a loving community."

Franklin helped found the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta. She said it's fitting such a foundational document got its public debut here.
